- **self**: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD (22/5)

## Definitions

- [statement] Multidisciplinary PD care is a patient-centered, needs-based model involving different professionals; the Parkinson Foundation describes experts working as needed across symptoms, while one randomized specialist-team model combined a movement-disorders specialist, PD nurses, and a social worker. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/finding-care · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23165981/

## How it works

- [statement] The national virtual-visit trial used a motor assessment that excluded rigidity and balance; the authors also identified difficulties assessing gait because of technology, camera view, and the absence of trained clinicians. Remote follow-up therefore leaves examination gaps. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] The 2017 national trial randomized 195 people and added 4 virtual specialist visits over 1 year to usual care. It reported 98% completing at least one virtual visit, 91% of scheduled virtual visits completed, and median savings of 88 minutes and 38 miles per visit. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] The 2026 Canoro narrative review identifies augmentation bias: telemedicine arms may receive more clinical attention than controls, so improvement cannot automatically be attributed to video delivery itself. The authors regard efficiency evidence and long-term economic sustainability as unresolved. (low confidence) — https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00702-026-03238-5 · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] The 2020 integrated-care review found only a small quality-of-life benefit in its outpatient subgroup; substantial overall heterogeneity and risk of bias limit generalization to all multidisciplinary models. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32598094/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] A nonrandomized trial found only small initial benefits from expert assessment and regional allied-health referrals; benefits disappeared after adjustment for baseline disease severity. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23988337/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] A 2022 review of multidisciplinary rehabilitation versus conventional physiotherapy included 6 studies and 1260 participants and found no statistically significant difference in functionality, disability, or quality of life. This rehabilitation comparison should not be treated as testing every integrated specialist-care model. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8901313/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] In a 2025 case-control study of 490 people with PD and 140 healthy controls, digital exclusion was greater in PD, especially because of poorer digital skills; PD severity independently predicted exclusion. These observational associations identify an implementation barrier rather than proving that PD causes digital exclusion. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12625107/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] A 2024 randomized study of fifty participants evaluated additional nurse, neurologist, and occupational-therapist telemedicine alongside office visits, reporting less frailty and improved quality of life. This is evidence for that small hybrid program, rather than proof that any video visit improves outcomes. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39586130/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] A nurse-managed PD clinic demonstrated a hybrid service design combining an onsite team with remote movement-disorder expertise and multidisciplinary referral. Its implementation report establishes feasibility and access experience, rather than a controlled estimate of clinical effectiveness. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26055776/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD

## Facts and statements

- [statement] In a randomized trial, 122 people were allocated to an 8-month specialist-team model or general-neurologist care; 100 completed follow-up. The team group improved on PDQ-39 and motor scores, but the authors cautioned that design limitations restricted interpretation. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23165981/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] Randomized PD telemedicine studies support reduced travel burden and convenient specialist follow-up; these access benefits should be evaluated separately from changes in clinical outcomes. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4909521/
- [statement] Neither the national add-on virtual-visit trial nor the VA follow-up trial demonstrated superior clinical outcomes with telemedicine. In the national trial, quality of life did not significantly improve; in the VA trial, clinical outcomes and overall patient satisfaction were similar between groups. These findings do not establish universal equivalence for all patients or services. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4909521/
- [statement] The national virtual-visit trial predominantly enrolled white, college-educated participants already familiar with the internet and frequently already receiving specialist care; its authors cautioned that results might not generalize to the broader PD population. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] The 2026 Canoro review recommends integrating televisits into validated hybrid care frameworks. This is consistent with the national trial authors proposing remote multidisciplinary services alongside clinic appointments and in-person home visits; the optimal combination remains a research question. (medium confidence) — https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00702-026-03238-5 · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/
- [statement] The 2026 Sun telehealth meta-analysis searched through June 21, 2024 and found heterogeneous quality-of-life results across intervention types and scales: pooled PDQ outcomes did not reach conventional statistical significance, whereas some other quality-of-life measures improved. Its broad intervention mix is not evidence that every virtual neurology visit improves quality of life. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12895161/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] A small 2024 survey combining autonomic-dysfunction and PD respondents reported high satisfaction with telehealth, but limited internet connectivity and impaired fine motor movements hindered access. Its mixed 25-person sample does not establish PD-wide satisfaction rates. (low confidence) — https://telehealthandmedicinetoday.com/index.php/journal/article/view/461/1075 · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] Published multidisciplinary-care findings differ by intervention and comparator: the van der Marck specialist-team trial was positive, whereas the Seid rehabilitation meta-analysis was null for quality of life; these are attributed findings from different care models, not a single universal treatment effect. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23165981/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8901313/
- [statement] Team-based PD care brings together different experts according to individual symptoms; integration can connect a specialist, a PD nurse, and a community neurologist through an individualized treatment plan. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/finding-care · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29392459/
- [statement] In the open-label randomized trial, an individualized plan and additional home visits coordinated by specialist, nurse, and community neurologist improved reported quality of life and motor/nonmotor symptoms over six months; durability and cost-benefit remained unanswered. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29392459/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] That national trial did not demonstrate improved quality of life from adding virtual visits to usual care, while saving a median 88 minutes and 38 miles per visit. A nonsignificant difference does not itself establish equivalence or noninferiority. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] Telemedicine delivery and multidisciplinary clinical content should be distinguished: the national trial delivered neurologist visits, whereas the hybrid trial added a multidisciplinary team to office care. Their different outcomes should not be pooled as though they tested the same service. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39586130/

## Research summary — Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD

Multidisciplinary PD care combines professionals around individual symptoms and needs. Some specialist-team models improve quality of life, but rehabilitation comparisons show inconsistent superiority. Virtual specialist visits can reduce travel and improve convenience without reliably improving clinical outcomes. Remote examinations have limits, and digital exclusion can disproportionately affect people with more advanced PD. Recent reviews favor carefully evaluated hybrid care and warn that additional clinical attention can confound comparisons between delivery modes. Evidence should distinguish access, patient experience, clinical effectiveness, and efficiency; it should also retain each study’s intervention, comparator, and population.

## Source disagreement — Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD

The specialist-team RCT and multidisciplinary-rehabilitation review report different quality-of-life results with different interventions and comparators; this limits blanket claims that every multidisciplinary model is superior.

Gate verdict: `SUPPORTED`. Auxiliary assertion: `prose:9a264477ae7fb3b3680abb4da97c0cbe5d030b6705e373eb2179dfca8b7755da`. Statement hash: `9a264477ae7fb3b3680abb4da97c0cbe5d030b6705e373eb2179dfca8b7755da`.
